title: EduMirror: Modeling Educational Social Dynamics with Value-driven Multi-agent Simulation
one_liner: Simulate school social interactions with psychologically grounded agents whose values shape behavior, then measure both visible actions and internal states to study interventions that would be hard or unethical to test directly.
lead: Educational researchers want to understand bullying, cooperation, peer influence, and classroom climate, but real-world experiments are often ethically constrained and observational data rarely supports strong causal claims. EduMirror offers a simulation environment in which many agents interact under configurable educational settings. Each agent is grounded in explicit psychological needs and social values, and the simulator measures both outward behavior and internal state. That makes the environment useful for controlled what-if studies of school dynamics.

problem.h2: Why educational social dynamics are hard to study
paras: School social behavior unfolds through many interacting factors: peer groups, status, values, unmet needs, classroom norms, and institutional rules. Researchers can observe these processes, but observation alone is weak for causal claims because many influences move together. Controlled experiments would help, but many interventions around bullying or exclusion are ethically unacceptable to run on real students because researchers cannot deliberately impose harmful social conditions on children.

A simulator could help, but only if the agents inside it behave in psychologically grounded ways because the simulator must connect internal motives to later behavior. If agent behavior is arbitrary or shallow, the simulation may produce vivid stories without scientific value. The challenge is to build agents whose actions and internal drives can be measured and manipulated in a structured way.

callout.html: Ground each simulated agent in explicit needs and social values, then track both observable behavior and internal state so interventions can be studied with clearer causal control.

panels.title: 1. Real school setting is hard to manipulate
panels.caption: Researchers cannot freely test harmful social interventions on real students.

steps.text: Choose the scenario, social roles, norms, and intervention conditions.
Assign each agent psychological needs, social value orientation, and role-specific context.
Let agents act, react, and update internal states across repeated encounters.
Record visible behavior and hidden internal states at the same time.
Run counterfactual conditions and observe how group dynamics change under each policy choice.

paras: The paper changes the level of grounding in educational multi-agent simulation. Instead of agents that only produce outward dialogue or actions, it adds explicit internal drives and a paired measurement protocol for visible and hidden social dynamics.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: internal social state
hidden.name: Unobserved psychological condition of each agent during interaction
paras: In real schools, researchers can observe teasing, helping, cooperation, silence, or withdrawal, but they often cannot directly observe internal conditions such as threat, belonging, frustration, or perceived fairness. Those internal conditions matter because they shape future behavior. EduMirror treats them as a first-class object of study.

The simulator estimates internal state from the agent design itself. Because each agent is built with explicit needs and values, the system can track how an interaction changes those hidden variables across time. This is useful because a policy may reduce visible conflict while increasing internal distress, or it may improve belonging before it changes outward behavior.

heat.caption: Darker means the internal state is stronger or more active in the current simulation round.

reads.html: The simulator tracks how students are doing internally, not only what they visibly say or do.
EduMirror uses value-driven agent forms and a dual-track measurement protocol so hidden psychological states can be analyzed alongside observable behavior.

paras: Social dynamics are not random exchanges of text. They are shaped by internal motives and constraints. A student who strongly values belonging may avoid open conflict even when treated unfairly. A student under high status pressure may join exclusionary behavior to preserve group position. If those drivers are absent, a simulator cannot directly study how interventions change group trajectories.

Value-driven agents help because they create structured links between inner state and outward action. When an intervention changes classroom norms, support access, or peer incentives, those changes alter internal needs and values, which in turn alter behavior across later rounds. The simulator becomes more scientifically useful because it can connect cause, internal response, and observed action in one controlled environment.

The paired measurement protocol is equally important. Researchers need to know not only whether bullying incidents fell, but why they fell and what side effects appeared internally. By tracking both behavior and hidden state, EduMirror can compare interventions more carefully because it distinguishes surface calm from genuine improvement in social conditions.

math.words: An agent's action tendency depends on its current internal state and its value profile. Interventions matter because they change those quantities over time, which then shifts future behavior probabilities.
symbols: preference score for one candidate action by agent a
current level of internal factor j for agent a, such as belonging or threat
importance of factor j in the agent's value profile

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: A student is choosing between support-a-peer and stay-silent.
Suppose belonging state = 0.8 and fairness state = 0.7.
If the agent values fairness strongly, the support action may score 0.6*0.8 + 0.7*0.7 = 0.97.
If the same agent also feels strong threat, a silence action may gain score from self-protection terms.
Behavior changes when interventions shift these internal states, so the simulator can study why the visible outcome moved.

math.note: The paper's full agent design is richer, but the central idea is that internal state and value weights jointly shape action choice across the simulation.

charts.title: Weakly grounded simulation
charts.note: A simulation without explicit psychological grounding is harder to trust for educational research.

charts.title: EduMirror
charts.note: Grounded agents and dual-track measurement improve scientific usefulness because visible behavior can be linked to internal mechanisms.

items.html: If the chosen needs and values leave out an important driver, the simulation may miss key dynamics because the internal state space is too coarse.

items.b: Evaluation focuses only on realism of dialogue.
items.html: A simulation can sound plausible while still misrepresenting social causality because fluent surface behavior does not guarantee that the internal mechanisms are well specified.
Even a grounded simulation is still a model, so policy conclusions must be qualified because unmodeled school factors may alter what happens in reality.

The method is most useful when researchers treat the simulator as a structured hypothesis-testing tool and validate both outward behavior and internal-state trends against educational theory and case evidence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a school-group simulation with roles such as target student, peer, bystander, and teacher. Define internal state variables such as belonging, threat, and trust. Run two scenarios such as baseline classroom practice and an intervention that increases teacher support and peer reporting. Measure visible incidents, cooperation, withdrawal, and the internal-state trends of each role over time.
demo.closing: The demo should show that a policy can be studied more carefully when the simulator records both visible group behavior and the internal psychological shifts that produce it.
